title: Beyond labour: Thengadi and the Kisan Sangh
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A trade unionist who thought farmers needed their own organisation.
body:
Dattopant Thengadi is best known for founding the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh in 1955. He also helped to found the **Bharatiya Kisan Sangh (BKS)**, which was announced as an all-India organisation at its first conference in Kota, Rajasthan, in March 1979. The two organisations tell us something about how he thought: that the worker and the farmer are not rivals but face a common problem. This post looks at his life and work, why he believed farmers needed an organisation of their own, what BKS has done, and what the Sangh family's three organisations share.

## A short portrait

Thengadi was born on 10 November 1920 in Arvi in the Wardha district of Maharashtra and died on 14 October 2004 in Pune. He studied at Morris College, Nagpur, and obtained a law degree. He became a full-time pracharak of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh in 1942. In the early 1950s he worked in the labour field as organising secretary of INTUC, then moved to other work. He served two terms in the Rajya Sabha from 1964 to 1976. Reference works say that he was awarded the Padma Bhushan and declined it.

BMS was founded on 23 July 1955, with the formation announced at a meeting in Bhopal, according to a tribute booklet published by BMS. The date is the birth anniversary of Lokmanya Tilak. Over the following decades he started or helped start a number of other bodies, including the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh, the Swadeshi Jagaran Manch, the Samajik Samarasata Manch, the Sarva Panth Samadar Manch and the Paryavaran Manch, and he co-founded the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad, the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat and the Bharatiya Vichara Kendra. He also wrote extensively; his books include *The Third Way*, *The Perspective* and *Labour Policy*.

## Why a farmers' organisation?

His reasoning, as BMS publications present it, was that workers and farmers face a common problem in a market where the producer is the weakest party. The farmer does not get a fair price for the crop, and the worker does not get a fair wage for the labour. Both need an organisation that speaks for the producer. The organisation he envisaged was one rooted in the farmer's own concerns and in national thought.

This links to a wider idea in his writing. He rejected the notion of class conflict as the basis of labour relations, and in his "Third Way" he sought an order that was neither capitalist nor socialist.

## The ideas behind the organisations

Thengadi's thinking is grounded in the "Integral Humanism" associated with Deendayal Upadhyaya. He treated labour's interests as part of the interests of the nation and rejected class conflict as the basis of labour relations. He contributed to labour policy documents, including a 1968 memorandum on labour policy and a 1969 National Charter of Demands of Indian Labour, according to the BMS tribute booklet. In 1974, according to a standard reference, he resigned as BMS's General Secretary to serve as secretary of the Lok Sangharsh Samiti, a step that is covered in the previous post on this blog. BMS today claims more than ten million members, while the figure in provisional Ministry of Labour statistics for 2002 was 6,215,797. Whichever figure one uses, the organisation he founded grew from a small beginning into one of the largest unions in the country.

## The founding of BKS

The reference record shows that the first BKS chapter in Rajasthan was formed in March 1978, and that the all-India organisation was announced on 4 March 1979 at its first All India Conference in Kota. The organisation uses a motto taken from the Rigveda, *Krishi Mit Krishaswa*, which means "do farming yourself". It describes itself as an organisation of farmers, for farmers, and as non-party, and it is generally counted among the organisations of the Sangh family.

## What BKS has campaigned for

BKS's agitations show what concerned farmers. In the 1980s, electricity prices were a central issue in Gujarat and Rajasthan. A 1985 rally at the Rajasthan Legislative Assembly was followed by a State decision to lower electricity prices, and there was an agitation in Gujarat in 1986-87 over drought and electricity prices. Later campaigns included a 2007 agitation in Saurashtra over cotton prices and the 2020 debate over the three agriculture bills, when BKS asked for modifications, including a referral of the bills to a parliamentary standing committee.

In broad terms, the positions associated with BKS are:

- **Remunerative prices** for farm produce, so that cultivation covers costs and leaves a living.
- Lower input costs, in particular for electricity.
- **Agricultural self-reliance** and a preference for practices suited to Indian conditions.
- Opposition to genetically modified crops, notably in oilseeds, without full safeguards.

These positions are those described in public accounts of the organisation. Readers who want the BKS's current demands should consult its own publications.

## The common thread

Thengadi's three best-known organisations, BMS, BKS and the later Swadeshi Jagaran Manch, are separate and autonomous, yet share three ideas: **nationalism, a constructive method and a focus on the producer.** "Constructive method" means that the organisation tries to build, to negotiate and to propose alternatives, and does not rest on opposition alone. The BMS slogan, which asks to industrialise the nation, "labourise" the industry and nationalise the labour, applies the same thought to industry: the worker is a stakeholder and not an outsider.

## A note on how he worked

Accounts by his associates describe Thengadi Ji as someone who kept himself in the background. The organisations he started did not carry his name, and he wanted others to carry them forward. Whether that is the full picture is for historians to judge, but the structure of these bodies, each with its own leaders and its own annual meetings, is consistent with it.

## What remains

Farm and factory face different problems today than in the 1950s and 1970s: price volatility, contract farming, mechanisation and migration from villages to cities. Agricultural labourers are among the largest groups in the unorganised workforce, and e-Shram data show agriculture accounting for about half of early registrations, so the concerns of the two organisations meet at many points. The question that Thengadi raised, who speaks for the producer, remains as relevant as ever.
